item.title: Family Firms as Context for Organizational Behavior Processes
item.content:encoded:
Melanie De Ruiter, Nyenrode Business University

Benjamin D. McLarty, Louisiana Tech University

Denise M. Rousseau, Carnegie Mellon University

James M. Vardaman, Memphis University

Despite calls to consider context in Organizational Behavior (OB) and management research, the broader OB and management literature has largely ignored family firms and the experiences and employment dynamics of their employees. OB research samples often are drawn without considering the nature of the settings involved or any potential impact on the variables of interest. Since family firms are a common type of business, ranging from sixty-five to ninety percent worldwide, samples in many OB and management studies likely conflate respondents from family and non-family firms. Such conflation can mask differences in behavioral processes that can result in erroneous inferences.

Treatment of family/non-family business as a dichotomous moderator only allows general differences to be noted without theoretically comparing psychological processes at the individual, team, and organizational levels. Moreover, since there is considerable heterogeneity within family firms, grouping employees working in different family firms together will likely forego important across family firm contextual differences in OB processes. Most studies in family firm research have been described as 'context-less'.

This special issue focuses on micro-OB processes in family firms, with the aim of extending recent endeavors on contextualizing family firm research by specifically focusing on the psychological and behavioral processes occurring within the family firm. Special attention is drawn to non-family employees in family firms, a prevalent group within the global workforce but surprisingly under-researched.

The special issue seeks answers to the questions: 'How do micro-OB concepts, processes and theories play out in family firm settings?', 'Why do micro-OB concepts, processes and theories play out in family firms in a particular way?' and 'How can an in-depth understanding of family firm phenomena extend knowledge or offer unique insights about micro-OB concepts, processes and theories?'. OB processes and outcomes that occur in family businesses are likely to be different from those found in non-family firms, yet family firm research is dominated by economic, financial and socio-economic frameworks often with little attention to OB-related phenomena.

To shed light on OB processes in family firms, scholars need theories of context to better specify OB dynamics characterizing family firms at the individual, team, and organizational levels and to compare these across family firms and to other kinds of firms. Scholars debate whether family firms are worse or better employers, with some arguing they are more conflict-filled because the goals of family and business systems may be at odds. However, informative contextual comparisons are largely lacking.

Articles should focus on meaningful theorizing about context and contextual differences in OB processes. Articles that focus on dichotomous family/non-family firm comparisons or simply conduct a study within a family firm without meaningful theorizing about context are not considered. Rather, articles should directly capture context through specific assessments to test measurement invariance and in-depth comparison of contextual differences, drawing from theories of context. The special issue welcomes data-based research articles, conceptual papers, reviews and critiques of research, and encourages qualitative research approaches for exploring emic concepts and heterogeneity within family firms.

Potential topics

  • Development and validation of measurement instruments (including assessment of measurement invariance) that allow a more generic assessment of contextual effects often put forward in family firm research (e.g., socioemotional wealth) to help theorize and understand similarities and differences in OB processes between family and non-family firms, and within family firms
  • Explicit tests of theories of context (e.g., trait activation theory; situation strength theory) to explain differences in relationships between personality traits and employee outcomes between family and non-family firms and within different types of family firms (e.g., enhanced understanding of family firm context as a driver for personality activation and impact on workplace performance and behaviors)
  • Development and validation of personality measurement instruments specific to the context of family for use in family firms, and meaningful contextual comparisons across family firms (including assessment of measurement invariance)
  • Enhanced theoretical understanding of how bifurcation bias based on family firm context as a potential motivational force for driving employee attitudes and behaviors
  • Multilevel research to better understand how the family firm context affects the extent to which leadership styles may (or may not) trickle down from family executives to family and non-family managers and in turn affect non-family employee outcomes in different types of family firms
  • An exploration of how critical events within the family firm context and family/non-family member dynamics shape employee and non-family manager perceptions and evaluations of their employment relationship with the family firm

Timeline

  • December 15, 2025: Proposal submission deadline
  • February 15, 2026: Decisions and feedback on proposals
  • February 1, 2027: Full manuscript submission deadline
  • May 1, 2027: Decisions and reviews on manuscripts
  • August 1, 2027: Revised manuscripts due
  • November 1, 2027: Second round decisions and reviews on revised manuscripts
  • February 1, 2028: Second round revised manuscripts due
  • April 1, 2028: SI editorial final review round and decisions on revised manuscripts
  • May 15, 2028: Final submissions of manuscripts
  • June 1, 2028: Final decision by guest editors
  • July 1, 2028: Accepted manuscripts to publisher

item.title: Advancing Management Research Through Theory Testing: A Special Issue of Replication and Reproducibility Studies
item.content:encoded:
William G. Obenauer, University of Maine

Robyn L. Brouer, University of South Alabama

Rachel Clapp-Smith, University of North Georgia

Ajay Rama Ponnapalli, Wayne State University

Andreas Schwab, Iowa State University

Jost Sieweke, Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam

Chen Wang, Western Michigan University

Group & Organizational Management (GOM) has made an explicit commitment to publishing replication research and contributing to an ecosystem that supports replication research in the organizational sciences. By making this commitment, GOM joins journals such as Strategic Management Journal, The Leadership Quarterly, Entrepreneurship: Theory and Practice, and Journal of Management Scientific Reports in this endeavor.

As part of GOM's commitment to supporting replication research, this special issue aims to stimulate a continued stream of replication and reproducibility submissions to GOM well beyond the publication of this special issue. Focal studies (i.e., studies replicated or reproduced) are not required to have been published in GOM, but they should be of interest to GOM's audience.

The special issue welcomes three types of submissions. Registered reports require researchers to submit their introduction and methods description before collecting data and will include detailed descriptions for either literal replication, literal reproducibility studies, or multi-study replication papers. Registered reports must include all methodological details as reviewers cannot grant acceptance in principle when methods lack transparency. Authors are encouraged to submit registered reports at least four months before the submission deadline to allow time for data collection. Importantly, authors must not collect data before their action editor gives acceptance in principle.

Literal replication or reproducibility study only submissions are limited to 2,000 words with limited introductions and discussion sections, with the majority of text focused on methodology and results. This recognizes the importance of bolstering the research record through literal replication and literal reproducibility studies.

Full-length submissions should use conceptual or constructive replication to advance knowledge through boundary testing or methodological improvements. Authors are encouraged to include reproducibility studies and/or literal replications within their full-length submissions for benchmarking purposes. While conducting a literal replication before constructive replication is encouraged, it is not required, as conducting reproducibility studies or literal replications may sometimes be infeasible due to practical constraints such as limited access to samples.

Potential topics

  • Registered reports on literal replications, literal reproducibility studies, or multi-study replication designs
  • Literal replication and reproducibility studies (single-study submissions)
  • Full-length submissions using conceptual or constructive replication to advance knowledge through boundary testing or methodological improvements
  • Reproducibility studies and literal replications for benchmarking purposes within full-length submissions
  • Replication research advancing organizational sciences

Timeline

  • June 30, 2027: Initial Submissions Due
